sources.title: 10 loại rêu hại thủy sinh: nguyên nhân và cách trị dứt điểm
6 Loại Rêu Hại Phổ Biến & Cách Xử Lý Tận Gốc Trong Hồ Thủy Sinh
RÊU HẠI VÀ CÁCH XỬ LÝ
Rêu hại hồ cá và hồ thủy sinh: Nguyên nhân và cách xử lý hiệu quả

facts.fact: Name for the term: "rêu hại"
Name for the term: "tảo"
Algae photosynthesise, turning light and nutrients such as fish waste into growth.
Algae give off oxygen by day and use oxygen at night.
Algae are not harmful in themselves and can act as a kind of filtration and as food for fish and invertebrates; most keepers dislike them for how they look.
A tank completely free of algae is unlikely.
Each kind of algae has its own causes, so identifying the kind comes before treating it.
Algae grow when light and nutrients are out of balance; sometimes the fix is more light or more nutrients rather than less.

Common causes listed are light that is too strong or on more than 8–10 hours a day, excess nutrients from overfeeding and waste, low CO2, an immature biofilter, infrequent water changes and weak flow.
Excess nutrients, low CO2, old bulbs and poor circulation are the main triggers named across algae kinds.
Target nutrient levels for planted tanks: N 10–20 ppm, P 0.5–2 ppm, K 10–20 ppm, Ca 10–30 ppm, Mg 2–5 ppm, Fe 0.1 ppm.
Keep CO2 at 20–30 ppm, as far as the fish and invertebrates allow.
Run lights 6–8 hours a day and never 24/7; cut light intensity by 30–40% when algae is heavy.
Light 8–10 hours a day, or 4–6 hours in a new tank; indirect sunlight counts toward this limit.
In a new tank, start with 5–6 hours of light a day and add 30 minutes weekly up to 8 hours.
Put the light on a timer so it stays constant, then adjust nutrients gradually, one change at a time, waiting at least 2–3 weeks to judge each change.
Change 30% of the water weekly, rising to twice weekly when algae appears.
Feed only what fish finish in 1–2 minutes.
Turn CO2 on 1 hour before the lights.
A Vietnamese shop warns that daylight in a bright room plus the tank light causes algae blooms, so do not run the light when the room is already very bright.
A Vietnamese shop notes that outdoor tanks in sunlight are prone to "rêu nước xanh".
A Vietnamese shop notes that silicate can already be present in tap water ("Silicat có thể có sẵn trong nước máy"), which feeds brown diatom algae.
A Vietnamese shop says "Rêu nhớt xanh" (cyanobacteria) is very common in Vietnam and most keepers meet it at least once.
Vietnamese shops name liquid carbon by the brands Excel and Cidex.
Copper algaecides will likely kill plants too.
Removing all nitrate from the water can trigger blue-green algae.
Treating only the visible algae without fixing the cause lets it come back.
Overusing hydrogen peroxide, running lights 24/7, overfeeding and changing 100% of the water are listed as common mistakes.
Strong chemicals can shock plants or set off another kind of algae.
Do not rinse filter media in tap water ("Không rửa vật liệu lọc bằng nước máy").
Algaecides harm plants and animals and should not be used casually.
Hydrogen peroxide: 1–2 ml per 10 liters, with the filter off for 15–20 minutes, applied directly on the algae; the algae turns white within 24 hours.
Bleach dip for algae-covered items: 1:20 bleach to water, then rinse until no bleach smell remains.
Excel or hydrogen peroxide can be spot-applied with a syringe onto algae.
Before spot-dosing liquid carbon or hydrogen peroxide, turn off the filter and stop the flow.
Otocinclus eat diatom algae.
Rêu tóc (genus Oedogonium): fine green hair-like threads on leaves, rocks, wood, substrate and glass.
Rêu tóc: caused by no CO2, excess nutrients, too much or too strong light and weak flow.
Hair/Thread Algae: caused by iron above 0.15 ppm.
Rêu tóc, rêu chỉ: caused by iron above 0.15 ppm.
Rêu Tóc, Rêu Chỉ: clears quickly once CO2 is right; remove by hand or tweezers and avoid iron-rich dosing early on.
Rêu tóc, rêu chỉ: the easiest algae to treat; some keepers grow it to feed fish.
Hair Algae: shorten the lighting period, increase fertilisation or reduce iron, and remove clumps with a toothbrush.
Rêu sừng hươu: dense clumps on leaf edges and veins, branching like antlers; harder to treat than rêu tóc.
Staghorn (Compsopogon sp.): caused by nutrient imbalance or low CO2; most fish and invertebrates will not eat it.
Tảo nâu (diatom, "tảo cát"): a brown slimy film on glass, rocks and wood, weakly attached.
Tảo nâu: low light plus high silicate, phosphate or nitrate.
Tảo nâu: in a new tank, wait 4–6 weeks for it to settle, or scrub it off.
Brown Diatom Algae: a dusty, flour-like brown coating on walls, substrate and surfaces, most often in newly planted tanks.
Brown Diatom Algae: caused by high phosphates and silicates.
Tảo Nâu: moderately raise light intensity or duration and change water regularly.
Rêu chùm đen (Audouinella, a red algae): black, dark green or dark red tufts on leaf edges, wood and rocks; it likes strong flow.
Rêu chùm đen: inject 3% hydrogen peroxide directly with a syringe at "1ml cho mỗi 2 lít nước".
Rêu Chùm Đen: low CO2 or weak flow is called the most common cause; also excess organics, excess iron, low pH and old leaves.
Rêu Chùm Đen: during treatment clean the filter and change 30% of the water every other day; it turns white or pink and disappears once CO2 is right.
Black Beard Algae: spray affected items out of the water with 3% hydrogen peroxide, leave 5 minutes, rinse and return; dying algae turns red or clear.
Black Beard Algae: can take six to eight months to establish, so removal takes a similarly long time.
Black Brush/Beard (Rhodophyta): caused by excess N, P or Fe, or by low pH.
GWAPA says the idea that BBA thrives in acidic water is only believed, not proven, and that African Rift tanks never get BBA is an anecdote from Neil Frank.
Rêu nước xanh: suspended algae, also called "tảo lam", that turn the water green and cloudy.
Rêu nước xanh: too much light is the main cause.
Green Water: cloudy pea-soup water from free-floating single-celled phytoplankton.
Green Water: too much light including direct sun, excess nutrients such as double-dosed fertiliser, or an ammonia spike.
Green Water: black out the tank for at least one week, or use a UV sterilizer, which kills it in about 2 to 3 days; large water changes do not work.
Green Water (Euglena): 5–10% water changes daily until clear, or 5 days without light.
Tảo Nước Xanh: lights off for 5–7 days with the tank fully covered, plus a UV sterilizer and more sponge filtration.
Tảo nước xanh: turn the light off and cover the tank for 5 days, called the best method.
Tảo nước xanh: does not harm plants or fish but spoils the look.
Rêu đốm xanh: small, hard green spots on glass, stone, wood and hard, large leaves.
Green Spot (Choleochaete orbicularis): caused by depleted phosphate.
Green Spot: dose phosphate up to 0.5–2.0 ppm.
Green Spot Algae: scrape with a razor blade on glass tanks or a gift card on acrylic tanks.
Rêu bụi xanh: a dusty green film on glass, loosely attached, that spreads to substrate, rocks and leaves.
Green Dust Algae (GDA): GDA has no confirmed cause; GWAPA gives a lifecycle of about 21 days.
Rêu nhớt xanh (Cyanobacteria): a thick carpet-like mat with bubbles underneath, dark green in freshwater; it is a bacterium, not an alga.
Blue-Green Algae: a slimy blanket over substrate, plants and decor with a distinctive smell; technically cyanobacteria.
Blue Green/Cyanobacteria: triggered by low nitrates, high organics, old bulbs or poor circulation.

Blue-Green Algae: improve circulation, remove it by hand, change water while vacuuming, then dose one packet of Maracyn (erythromycin) per 10 gallons and wait one week before a water change; repeat once if needed.
Blue Green: raise nitrate to about 5 ppm; Maracyn (erythromycin) at half dosage kills it.
Rêu nhớt xanh: raise nitrates to 5 ppm, add fast-growing plants and turn off the light.
Rêu Nhớt Xanh: siphon off the slime, turn lights off for 3–5 days and increase aeration.
Blue-Green Algae: a week-long blackout is hard on plants, and algae eaters typically will not eat it.
Cladophora: tough green wool-like mats, possibly brought in on Marimo balls.
Rêu chùm (Cladophora): looks like hair algae but is a different species; moss balls can carry it, and it is hard to treat.
Rêu xoăn (Fuzz Algae): curly tufted growth on leaf edges, from nutrient imbalance or low CO2.
Rêu trắng: white growth that is fungus on leftover food or new driftwood, or a bacterial film on substrate; it does not photosynthesise, so reducing light does not help.
